summary: Jesus tells of a king whose invited guests refuse his son’s wedding feast, who fills the hall from the highways, and who expels a guest without a wedding garment.
key_insight: The hall was filled with guests gathered from the highways, “both bad and good”; no one there had earned a seat. Yet the king still looked for a wedding garment. The invitation was free, but it was not casual. Guests came on the king’s terms, not their own.
story: Jesus answered the leaders again with a parable. “The kingdom of heaven is like a certain king who arranged a marriage for his son.” He sent out his servants to call those who had been invited, but they were not willing to come.

He sent other servants with a fuller message: “See, I have prepared my dinner; my oxen and fatted cattle are killed, and all things are ready. Come to the wedding.” But they made light of it and went their ways, one to his own farm, another to his business. The rest seized his servants, treated them spitefully and killed them.
When the king heard about it, he was furious. He sent out his armies, destroyed those murderers and burned up their city.

Then he said to his servants, “The wedding is ready, but those who were invited were not worthy. Therefore go into the highways, and as many as you find, invite to the wedding.” The servants went out and gathered all they found, both bad and good, and the wedding hall was filled with guests.

When the king came in to see the guests, he saw a man there who did not have on a wedding garment. “Friend, how did you come in here without a wedding garment?” he asked. The man was speechless. Then the king told the servants, “Bind him hand and foot, take him away, and cast him into outer darkness; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.”
Jesus ended, “For many are called, but few are chosen.”

fit.question: Luke tells a parable of a great supper whose invited guests make excuses, so the host brings in the poor and the outsiders (Luke 14:16–24). Is Matthew’s wedding feast the same parable?

points.label: Two settings
points.text: Luke’s parable was told earlier, at a Pharisee’s table on the way to Jerusalem (event 106). Matthew’s was told in the temple in the last week, right after the parable of the tenants.

points.label: Two different stories
points.text: In Luke a man gives a supper and the guests make polite excuses. In Matthew a king gives a wedding feast for his son, the guests kill his servants, armies burn their city, and a guest without a wedding garment is thrown out. Jesus, like any teacher, could use a familiar picture more than once and shape it for a new moment.

fit.note: Similar pictures on different occasions make two parables, not one remembered two ways.
fit.short: Different settings and different stories. Jesus told the great supper earlier and the wedding feast in the temple in His last week.

scene.label: Two invitations
scene.text: Guests to a great feast were invited ahead of time and then called again when everything was ready; when Esther gave her banquet, the king’s servants came “and hastened to bring Haman” (Esther 6:14). To accept the first invitation and refuse the second was an insult to the host.

scene.label: A burned city
scene.text: A king sending armies against people who refused a wedding seems out of scale, and that is the point: refusing the king’s son was rebellion. Many readers hear in Matthew 22:7 a warning of what happened to Jerusalem in AD 70, about forty years later.

scene.label: The wedding garment
scene.text: Scholars debate whether hosts supplied festive garments to guests; the evidence for such a custom is uncertain. What the story makes clear is that the man had no excuse: he was “speechless.” Isaiah rejoiced that God “has clothed me with the garments of salvation” (Isaiah 61:10).

scene.label: Outer darkness
scene.text: Wedding feasts often ran on into the night, in halls bright with lamps. To be thrown out was to be thrown into the dark. Matthew records Jesus using the phrase three times, always for final judgment (8:12; 22:13; 25:30).

witnesses.matthew: Only Matthew tells this parable, the third of three he sets together after the leaders challenged Jesus’ authority. It moves from the vineyard to the banquet hall: the son is now the bridegroom, the invited guests refuse, and the hall fills with people from the highways. Matthew keeps both sides, the wide-open door and the warning about coming unprepared, as he does elsewhere (7:21–23).

seeing.reveals: Jesus is the King’s Son for whom the feast is made. The invitation goes out in His name, and the parable turns on how people respond to the wedding of the Son.
seeing.living: Some guests refused with violence; others were simply busy with a farm or a business. Treating God’s invitation as one more appointment is as fatal as fighting it. And those who do come must be ready to be clothed as the King requires.
seeing.ponder: What ordinary business has made you treat the King’s invitation lightly?

preaching.big_idea: The King’s invitation is free and wide, but no one may come on his own terms.
preaching.watch_for: The parable turns twice: from the refused guests to the highways (v. 8), and from the full hall to one man without a garment (v. 11). Preach both turns. The open door and the inspection belong to the same story.
